in FS, the reabsorption defect of filtered polypeptides by renal proximal cells results in the appearance of several proteins of renal origin, and in the urinary loss of proteins of plasma origin that are normally reabsorbed.
the urinary proteome in Dent's patients, compared to normal subjects, shows a relative increase in plasma proteins and a relative decrease in proteins of renal origin.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the specificity of the proximal reabsorption of filtered proteins.
understanding the mechanisms of proteinuria in FS and the pathophysiology of Dent's disease.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the renal proximal tubular cell is not only a barrier for reabsorption but also for secretion of polypeptides, a function that is impaired in renal FS.
the proximal tubular epithelium has a specific role in reabsorption, which is impaired in Dent's disease.
the urinary proteome in FS reflects the specific function of the proximally located nephron segment, which is the first to encounter the filtered polypeptides.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
in Dent's FS, the proximal tubular dysfunction is not a general one but rather specific for certain classes of proteins, and that these proteins are reabsorption targets of the nephron.
Dent's patients, due to a CLC-5 mutation, have a defective endocytosis of filtered proteins, which are normally reabsorbed by the proximal tubules.
in FS there is a selective failure to reabsorbs some polypeptides, which are normally endocytosed by the renal proximal tubular cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the proximal tubular cells have the capacity to discriminate among polypeptides, and that the urinary proteome reflects this specificity.
the proximal tubular cells of the human nephron are highly selective with regard to which polypeptides they reabsorb.
the renal proximal tubular epithelium is not only involved in the reabsorptive process but also in the regulation of the plasma proteome.
